questions.q: What is the first step in Shor's algorithm's pipeline, and why does it matter?
options: Classically factor N directly, skipping the quantum circuit entirely
Immediately measure the counting register before any quantum operation
Classically pick a random a coprime to N, checked via gcd -- if gcd(a, N) > 1, a factor has already been found for free
Apply the inverse QFT before initializing any register
questions.explain: Step 1 is cheap classical preprocessing: choosing a and verifying gcd(a, N) = 1, with the rare lucky case of gcd(a,N) > 1 handled immediately.

questions.q: What does the controlled modular exponentiation unitary U_a implement, and why is it the expensive part of the circuit?
options: It implements a simple bit-flip on the work register, costing O(1) gates regardless of N's size
It implements the inverse QFT itself, making steps 3 and 4 identical
It directly outputs the prime factors of N without any further processing
It implements |x⟩|y⟩ → |x⟩|y·a^x mod N⟩ via chained controlled modular multiplications, costing roughly O(n^3) gates for an n-bit N -- the dominant resource cost
questions.explain: Modular exponentiation is built from O(n) controlled modular multiplications, each costing roughly O(n^2) gates, dominating total circuit size at roughly O(n^3) gates.

questions.q: Why are steps 2 through 4 (superposition, controlled modular exponentiation, inverse QFT) described as 'phase estimation applied to U_a'?
options: Because phase estimation and modular exponentiation are unrelated procedures that happen to share a name
Because step 3 replaces phase estimation entirely with a lookup table

Because U_a's eigenvalues encode the unknown period r as a phase e^(2*pi*i*k/r), and the Hadamard-then-inverse-QFT pattern is exactly the general phase estimation procedure from earlier chapters, specialized to this unitary
Because the inverse QFT is only used for visual display of results, not for extracting any numeric value
questions.explain: Shor's period-finding circuit is a direct, specialized instance of the general phase estimation algorithm applied to the unitary U_a, whose eigenstructure encodes the period.

questions.q: After measuring the counting register, what classical step recovers the exact period r, and why is it needed?
options: The continued-fractions algorithm, because the measurement only yields a value close to a multiple of 2^n/r, not r itself exactly
A second full run of the quantum circuit with a different a, discarding the first measurement entirely
Classical trial division of N by every integer up to sqrt(N)
No further step is needed; the measured value directly equals r
questions.explain: The measured value approximates s*2^n/r for an unknown integer s; continued fractions extracts the best rational approximation s/r, recovering the candidate period r.

questions.q: Once r is recovered, what is the final step of the pipeline?
options: Re-run the entire quantum circuit from scratch with a larger counting register
Classically check that r is even and a^(r/2) is not congruent to -1 (mod N), then compute gcd(a^(r/2) - 1, N) and gcd(a^(r/2) + 1, N) to extract the factors
Apply the QFT a second time to the work register
Report N as prime if r is odd, with no further checking
questions.explain: This final step reuses exactly the algebraic reduction proved in Lesson 21: check the evenness and -1 conditions, then extract factors via gcd.
